name: Against Malaria Foundation: insecticide-treated nets (charityevals)
summary: The Against Malaria Foundation buys long-lasting insecticidal nets for mass campaigns that governments and partners distribute; in its financial year to June 2025 it funded 75.3 million nets for the DRC, Nigeria, South Sudan, Chad, Guinea and Zambia for $178 million, nets for about 136 million people. Valuing the malaria deaths, illness and stillbirths averted and children's later earnings by the site's standard steps, with credit shared with the partners who pay for distribution, this comes to about 25 years of healthy life per $1,000: more than half from lives saved, mostly of young children, and nearly two-fifths from children's later earnings. The biggest uncertainties are how much today's nets cut malaria deaths now that mosquitoes resist pyrethroids, how much schooling and earnings children gain, and how long nets last in the household.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Spending on net distributions in FY2025 (July 2024 to June 2025): all charitable activities

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)
source.page: p.21, Statement of Financial Activities; note 3

rows.explainer: All of AMF's FY2025 expenditure is on its one programme, long-lasting insecticidal nets: nets ($171,957,961), non-net costs it funds, mostly post-distribution monitoring ($4,974,347), central costs ($1,041,315), governance ($29,629) and a foreign-exchange loss ($8,571). FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025) is the latest year with audited accounts; FY2026's accounts are still being audited. AMF books a grant of nets when the agreement is signed, so these are the nets committed in the year, distributed over the following months and years.

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)

rows.explainer: Total expenditure for FY2025 from the same audited statements. AMF has no separate fundraising or management line: central costs are inside charitable activities.

rows.label: Programme expenses (all programmes), FY2025

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)

rows.explainer: Charitable activities, the whole of AMF's spending; its central costs are already included, so the overhead multiplier is 1.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost. For AMF it is 1: its central costs are part of charitable activities.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled program, including overhead
Nets funded in FY2025 (grants of nets agreed in the year)

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)
source.page: p.30, note 5 (Grants of LLINs: Chad 8,272,050; DRC 29,085,845; Guinea 4,751,550; Nigeria 19,045,150; South Sudan 9,502,210; Zambia 4,675,350)

rows.explainer: Nets AMF committed to in FY2025, by country: DRC 39%, Nigeria 25%, South Sudan 13%, Chad 11%, Guinea 6%, Zambia 6%. These shares weight the country figures below. AMF's own count; distribution and use are checked by its post-distribution monitoring (below, in the retention and delivery rows).

rows.label: People with access per net (AMF's allocation figure)

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, AMF's funding gap
source.quote: 1.80 (# of people that sleep under each net)

rows.explainer: AMF's planning figure, also behind its 'people protected' counter (853.6 million people for 474.2 million nets, 1.80). AMF calls it the people who sleep under each net; in fact it is the allocation, one net per two people rounded up per household, so it counts people with access. The use rate and AMF's coverage surveys below turn access into nights actually slept under a net, as in Bertozzi-Villa's definitions, so use is not discounted twice. The range allows for small and crowded households.

rows.label: People reached in the year modelled (people with access to the nets funded)
rows.explainer: People given access to the nets funded in FY2025, at AMF's 1.8 per net; the coverage rows below turn access into nights under a net.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context: AMF's own spending per person protected, nets plus monitoring and central costs; partners' distribution costs are not in it (they lower the credit share instead).

rows.label: AMF's cost per net funded, all its costs included
rows.explainer: About $2.36: the net itself (AMF says close to $2.00 now; $2.28 on average in FY2025) plus monitoring and central costs.

rows.label: Years a net stays in the household (mean retention, AMF's six countries)

source.title: Bertozzi-Villa et al. 2021, Nature Communications 12:3589, Supplementary Information, Table 1.7 (LLIN median retention times) and Note 1 (net loss function)

rows.explainer: Median retention fitted to national surveys for each of AMF's FY2025 countries, weighted by its nets: 1.525 years. Expected years need the mean, not the median: the paper's loss curve, exp(κ − κ / (1 − (t/τ)²)) with κ fixed at 20, has a mean 1.045 times its median (computed numerically), so 1.59. South Sudan and Chad sit at the model's 1-year prior floor with 1 to 3 surveys, so the range is wide (1.3 to 2.3, about the 40-country interquartile range of 1.33 to 2.37). This is the cross-country side of the blend below; AMF's own monitoring is the other.

rows.label: Share of people with a net who sleep under it

source.title: Bertozzi-Villa et al. 2021, Nature Communications 12:3589
source.quote: The use rate has increased with small fluctuations across the time series examined, from a low of 71.3% (67.6–75.1) in 2004 to a 2020 estimate of 87.1% (83.1–90.3).

rows.explainer: Use among those with access to a net, Africa 2020, with its 95% interval. Nets are used less in the dry season; the figure is a yearly average.

rows.label: Years of use per person, cross-country survey model (retention × use)
rows.explainer: Years a person with access to a new net sleeps under it, from Bertozzi-Villa et al.'s fits to national surveys: mean retention in AMF's six countries (1.59 years) times use among those with access.

rows.label: Years of use per person, AMF's own post-distribution monitoring (to the 36-month replacement)

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)
source.quote: sleeping space coverage on day 1 (immediately post distribution) of around 95%, falling to 85-75% after 9 months, to 80-70% after 18 months and to 65-50% after 27 months

rows.explainer: AMF's surveys of a sample of its own distributions, at 9, 18 and 27 months: the share of sleeping spaces covered by a hung net. A hung net over a sleeping space already measures use, so this is not multiplied by the use rate. Integrating the mid-points (95%, 80%, 75%, 57.5%, and about 45% at 36 months, extrapolated past the last survey) over the three years until the next campaign gives about 2.1 coverage-years; AMF's low and high bands give 1.96 and 2.28, and the range 1.8 to 2.4 adds the extrapolation's uncertainty. Collected by AMF's partners on 1.5% samples, so less independent than national surveys.

rows.label: Weight on AMF's own monitoring against the cross-country model
rows.explainer: Our judgment: half each. AMF's surveys are of its own nets and countries, but partner-collected on small samples, and 'hung' at an announced or semi-announced visit can overstate use; the cross-country model is independent but averages 40 countries and other distribution channels.

rows.label: Years of protection per person reached
rows.explainer: A blend of AMF's own monitoring and the cross-country model: the years a person with access to an AMF net actually sleeps under it. Waning insecticide over the net's life is in the external-validity adjustment, not here.

rows.label: Malaria deaths per person-year in AMF's FY2025 countries (all ages, 2024)

source.title: WHO, World Malaria Report 2025, Annex 4-H: population at risk and estimated malaria cases and deaths, 2000-2024
source.quote: Deaths Point 2024: DRC 67,676; Nigeria 184,933; South Sudan 6,749; Chad 13,862; Guinea 10,245; Zambia 8,682 (population at risk 109.3m; 232.7m; 11.9m; 20.1m; 14.8m; 21.3m)

rows.explainer: WHO's estimated malaria deaths in 2024 divided by the population at risk, country by country, weighted by AMF's FY2025 nets: DRC 0.62, Nigeria 0.79, South Sudan 0.57, Chad 0.69, Guinea 0.69, Zambia 0.41 per 1,000 a year, 0.656 overall. Low and high use WHO's lower and upper estimates (0.46 and 1.01). These are direct malaria deaths in today's population, so they already reflect the fall in malaria mortality since the trials of the 1990s; indirect deaths are added below. AMF targets high-burden areas within these countries, so the national average may understate the risk (in the range).

rows.label: Share of the population with access to a net today, AMF's countries (2024)

source.title: WHO, World Malaria Report 2025, Annex 4-G: commodities distribution and coverage, 2022-2024
source.quote: Modelled percentage of population with access to an ITN, 2024: Chad 57.6; DRC 69.9; Guinea 53.1; Nigeria 47.7; South Sudan 65.4; Zambia 70.7

rows.explainer: WHO's modelled access in 2024, weighted by AMF's FY2025 nets per country: 61.3%. Used only to turn today's death rate, which already includes the protection of the nets in use, into the death rate of people without a net.

rows.label: Share of the population sleeping under a net today
rows.explainer: Access times use among those with access.

rows.label: Reduction in malaria deaths among people sleeping under a net

source.title: Pryce, Richardson, Lengeler 2018, Insecticide-treated nets for preventing malaria, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD000363.pub3
source.quote: A 44% reduction in the incidence of severe malaria episodes was seen in the ITN group (rate ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.82; 2 trials, 31,173 participants, high-certainty evidence)

rows.explainer: Cochrane's pooled effect of nets against no nets on severe malaria, the episodes that kill, standing in for direct malaria deaths (the review reports no malaria-specific mortality); its 95% interval as the range. The same review finds 45% fewer uncomplicated P. falciparum episodes (rate ratio 0.55) and 17% lower all-cause child mortality (0.83, 0.77 to 0.89; 5.6 lives a year per 1,000 children protected). Checked against that all-cause result: with control-arm child mortality of about 33 per 1,000 (5.6 ÷ 0.17) and direct malaria about a quarter of it, 0.44 × 8 per 1,000 × (1 + the shared indirect ratio below, 0.75) gives about 6.2 per 1,000, inside the trials' 3.6 to 7.6.

rows.label: Malaria death rate without a net, relative to today's average
rows.explainer: Today's death rate is an average over people with and without nets. People who would otherwise go without die at a higher rate: the average divided by (1 − share using a net × the net's effect). Whether they would in fact go without is the counterfactual adjustment.

rows.label: Deaths malaria causes indirectly, per direct malaria death
rows.explainer: Malaria also kills indirectly, through anaemia, low birthweight and weakened resistance to other infections, deaths not counted as malaria. The site's one figure for this (@givewell.indirect_malaria_deaths_per_direct_malaria_death_2, 0.75), as in the SMC models. Cross-check against the trials: with control-arm child mortality of about 33 per 1,000 and direct malaria about a quarter of it, 0.44 × 8 × 1.75 gives about 6.2 deaths averted per 1,000 child-years, inside Cochrane's all-cause 3.6–7.6 (point 5.6).

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Malaria deaths per person-year without a net × the net's effect × (1 + indirect deaths) × years under the net. Nets protect everyone under them, so the rate is for all ages; the age split of the deaths follows.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: WHO's Global Health Estimates for malaria deaths by age in AMF's six countries, weighted by its nets: 76% under five (@death_ages.malaria_amf_fy2025_share_under5). WHO's World Malaria Report gives 75% for the African Region, consistent. Indirect deaths are valued at the same age mix as direct ones; if they are more concentrated under five, as is likely, this slightly undervalues them.

rows.label: Malaria illness averted, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Nets also avert about half of uncomplicated malaria episodes (Cochrane rate ratio 0.55) and raise haemoglobin. The site's one figure for malaria illness averted by nets and SMC (@givewell_common.malaria_morbidity), a share of all modelled value (deaths, stillbirths and income) as in the SMC models, added alongside the other supplemental shares. Not also counted in the unmodelled benefits row.

rows.label: Births per person per year, AMF's FY2025 countries

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Birth rate, crude (per 1,000 people), SP.DYN.CBRT.IN
source.quote: 2024: DRC 40.885, Guinea 33.325, Nigeria 32.493, South Sudan 29.222, Chad 43.264, Zambia 32.724

rows.explainer: Crude birth rates for 2024, weighted by AMF's FY2025 nets per country: 36.6 per 1,000 people a year.

rows.label: Stillbirths per live birth, AMF's FY2025 countries

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Stillbirth rate (per 1,000 total births), SH.DYN.STLB (UN IGME)
source.quote: 2023: DRC 25.9, Guinea 22.7, Nigeria 23.9, South Sudan 27.6, Chad 28.4, Zambia 14

rows.explainer: UN IGME's 2023 stillbirth rates, weighted by AMF's FY2025 nets per country: 24.9 per 1,000 total births, which is 0.0256 per live birth (24.9 ÷ 975.1), because the birth rate above counts live births.

rows.label: Reduction in stillbirths among women sleeping under a net
rows.explainer: Gamble et al.'s Cochrane review (CD003755.pub2) found nets reduced stillbirths and abortions in first to fourth pregnancies by a third in Africa (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.97), but not in later ones. Our judgment halves that to 15% for all births: about a third of births are fifth pregnancies or later, part of the fetal loss counted was early abortion, and most women now also get preventive treatment in pregnancy. The trial's upper effect is the high end.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Births per person-year × stillbirths per birth × the net's effect × years under the net.

rows.label: Share of people reached who are children (under 15)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Population ages 0-14 (% of total population), SP.POP.0014.TO.ZS
source.quote: 2025: DRC 45.95, Guinea 40.55, Nigeria 40.52, South Sudan 37.99, Chad 45.96, Zambia 40.97

rows.explainer: Weighted by AMF's FY2025 nets per country: 42.9%. Only children's later earnings are counted.

rows.label: Extra years of schooling per child-year under a net
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on Barofsky, Anekwe and Chase (2015, Journal of Health Economics), who find that Uganda's 1959–60 eradication campaign 'raised educational attainment by about a half year' for children exposed in early childhood: about 0.1 to 0.2 years per year of near-elimination, times nets' 45% cut in malaria, is 0.05 to 0.09; we halve it (0.03) for a single quasi-experiment, publication bias and partial rather than full protection. Bleakley (2010) finds higher adult income in cohorts born after eradication in the Americas, in the same direction.

rows.label: Increase in earnings per year of schooling, ln(consumption)

source.title: Psacharopoulos and Patrinos 2018, Returns to investment in education: a decennial review of the global literature, Education Economics 26(5):445-458
source.quote: the private average global rate of return to one extra year of schooling is about 9 percent a year

rows.explainer: The global average private return to a year of schooling, about 9% (as a log gain); higher in low-income countries, lower once ability bias is removed, hence 6–12%.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, ln(consumption) per year
rows.explainer: Children's share of the people reached × child-years under the net × extra schooling per child-year × the earnings return to schooling: the yearly gain in ln(consumption) in adulthood, per person reached, undiscounted.

rows.label: Years until the income gain starts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for the wait between malaria prevention in childhood and the start of adult earnings (@givewell_shared.years_until_income_benefits_malaria).

rows.label: Years the long-term income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Later-life income gain per person reached, present value
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included, so the result moves with it. Never type in a present value worked out elsewhere: rebuild it from its inputs.

rows.label: Resource sharing within households (multiplier on an earner's gain)
rows.explainer: An adult's higher earnings are shared with the household, so the gain in consumption reaches more people than the earner: the site's one figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier), as every model valuing a childhood health programme's income gain uses.

rows.label: Internal validity of the malaria trials, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for the internal validity of the malaria trials behind nets and SMC (@givewell_common.internal_validity_adjustment_malaria): 23 randomised trials with high-certainty evidence for mortality and severe malaria (Cochrane 2018).

rows.label: External validity: trials of the 1990s against today's nets and mosquitoes, a multiplier
rows.explainer: The trials ran in 1987–2001, before mosquitoes became widely resistant to pyrethroids, and on nets re-treated during the trials, while today's nets lose insecticide over their life and mosquitoes in several of AMF's countries bite earlier or outdoors. AMF now buys mostly PBO and dual-active-ingredient (chlorfenapyr) nets, which trials in Tanzania and Benin found more effective than standard nets where resistance is high, restoring part of the loss. Our judgment: 0.8 (0.6 if resistance erodes most of the gain, 0.95 if the new nets fully restore it). Falling malaria mortality since the trials is already in the baseline row; how long nets are used is in the coverage rows.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Internal validity (the site's malaria figure) times external validity (our judgment).

rows.label: Share of the protection that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: AMF's nets replace those of the previous campaign, roughly three years earlier. AMF's own monitoring finds 50–65% of sleeping spaces still covered at 27 months, so some old nets remain; but campaigns registered with AMF count 'sleeping spaces and existing, useable LLINs' before allocating nets (accounts, accounting policy f), the old nets left are torn and low on insecticide, and continuous channels (antenatal and immunisation clinics, schools) and private purchases cover a few more. Our judgment: 75% of the net-years AMF provides are additional (60–90%). Whether another funder would have paid for the campaign is the leverage and funging row, not this one.

rows.label: Partners' cost per net for shipping, registration and distribution

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, AMF's funding gap
source.quote: This is based on the cost of a distributed net being US$4.50. Non-net costs = shipping, household registration and net distribution costs

rows.explainer: AMF pays for the nets; co-funding partners (governments, the Global Fund, others) pay to ship, register households and hand them out (AMF, Monitoring costs page: 'AMF typically funds the cost of the nets and co-funding partners fund all distribution non-nets costs'). AMF's own figure for a distributed net, $4.50, less its $2.00 net, leaves $2.50. Scates et al. (2020, Malaria Journal) costed two 2015 mass campaigns in Mali at $4.37 and $4.61 per net distributed (economic cost, 2016 dollars) with the net the largest item, implying about $1.5 to $2 of delivery: the low end.

rows.label: AMF's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: AMF's cost per net over the full cost of a delivered net, AMF's plus its partners'. Partners' money is not in the cost (Convention 2); it lowers AMF's share of the credit instead, in both credit modes.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (nets lost outside what the coverage sources measure)
rows.explainer: Both coverage sources already count nets that never reach households: AMF's monitoring measures sleeping-space coverage in registered households (95% on day 1), and Bertozzi-Villa's retention is fitted from nets distributed against nets found in household surveys. So the best guess is 1. The low end, 95%, allows for a large theft or conflict loss outside the monitoring samples (AMF's accounts report one, 45,000 nets in FY2020; eastern DRC and South Sudan are hardest to monitor).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Below 1 when governments or other funders would have bought these nets without AMF. AMF funds only distributions with a verified gap after other funders' pledges, and its funding-gap page puts the gap for 2024–26 campaigns 'significantly in excess of US$300m after all major funders' contributions'; the 2025 cuts in US malaria funding widened gaps. Some campaigns would still have been funded later or partly by others. Our judgment: 0.93 (0.75–1.0). Partners' distribution money is in the credit share, not here.

rows.label: Years a donation waits in AMF's balance before it is granted

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Financial information (easier-to-understand accounts), and the FY2025 accounts note 16 (funds)

rows.explainer: AMF holds money for nets until a distribution is agreed, and grants are lumpy. In FY2025 alone the balance held to buy nets averaged ($129.2m + $85.9m) ÷ 2 = $107.6m against $172.0m of nets granted, 0.63 years (the low end); over FY2024 to FY2026 the year-end balance averaged about $210m against $77.8m a year of grants, 2.7 years (the high end, inflated by FY2026's large gift and small grants, which FY2027's $215m granted so far is drawing down). Best guess 1.2 years.

rows.label: Interest earned on AMF's cash while donations wait, a yearly rate

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)
source.page: p.21 SOFA; note 15, total cash and cash equivalents 285,213,362 (2024: 184,559,223)

rows.explainer: Interest of $12.37m over average cash of ($184.6m + $285.2m) ÷ 2 = $234.9m: 5.3% in FY2025. AMF uses '100% of any interest earned on public donations' to buy nets (accounts, funds note), so a dollar that waits buys more nets; the low end allows for falling deposit rates.

rows.label: Years from AMF's grant to the nets being in use
rows.explainer: AMF books a grant when agreed. At year end 21.4 million nets were being distributed, 62.6 million were scheduled within 12 months and 7.0 million after (accounts p.7, distribution status): about half a year after year end, so about a year after the average grant date. Our judgment: 1.0 year (0.5–2.0).

rows.label: Years from distribution to the middle of the nets' use
rows.explainer: The protection is spread over the nets' life; half the coverage years approximates when the average night of protection happens.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the nets are in use
rows.explainer: The wait from a gift to AMF's grant, from the grant to the nets being in use, and to the middle of their use, discounted at the shared rate like every future benefit; the interest a waiting donation earns, which buys more nets, offsets the first wait.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * delay_discount
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Treatment costs averted, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Cases prevented save households and clinics the cost of treating them, money that goes to other uses. The site's one figure for prevention programmes (@givewell_shared.treatment_costs_averted).

rows.label: Protection of people not under the nets, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Insecticidal nets kill mosquitoes, so at high coverage neighbours without nets are protected too; the Asembo Bay trial in Kenya (Hawley et al. 2003) found such a community effect on child mortality. Three things keep it small here: cluster-randomised trials already capture much of it inside the clusters; AMF's campaigns cover about 95% of sleeping spaces at the start, leaving few non-users; and, as Okumu (2020, Malaria Journal, doi 10.1186/s12936-020-03321-6) writes, 'Widespread resistance in African malaria vectors has greatly weakened the historical mass mosquitocidal effects' of nets. Our judgment: +5% (0 to 20%).

rows.label: Harms and risks (misuse, faster insecticide resistance), as a share of value lost
rows.explainer: A negative share: nets used for fishing (with insecticide in water) or discarded, and some added pressure towards resistance. Our judgment: −2% (−5% to 0).

rows.label: Rebound malaria from lost immunity, as a share of value lost
rows.explainer: Children protected from infection build immunity more slowly and may get more malaria later: the site's one figure for nets and SMC (@givewell_common.rebound_effects_decreased_immunity_development), a negative share.

rows.label: Investment of income increases, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Part of the later income gain is invested and yields returns: the site's figure for nets (@givewell_shared.investment_of_income_increases_nets), half the default for most programmes.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The rows above: treatment costs averted (+), protection of non-users (+), harms (−), rebound from lost immunity (−), investment of income gains (+). Illness itself is in the morbidity row, not here.

rows.label: Deaths averted
Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age band of each death averted (under five, 5–14, 15–49, 50 and over), weighted by the malaria age mix of AMF's countries (@death_ages.malaria_amf_fy2025_share_*, WHO GHE 2023), times your multiplier on the value of a life: the site's one value of a death (docs/normalization.md 2.7).

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
Units of value from illness averted
Units of value from stillbirths averted
rows.explainer: A stillbirth averted at the site's one value (@givewell_shared.uov_per_stillbirth, GiveWell's), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

rows.label: Units of value from later-life income
Total units of value
Units of value per dollar
AMF staff costs, FY2025

source.title: Against Malaria Foundation, Annual Report and Financial Statements for the year ended 30 June 2025 (audited, global consolidated)
source.quote: Staff costs cover the cost of 14 individuals (12 salaried) employed by the charity during the year

rows.explainer: Salaries, pensions, social security and programme support for AMF's 14 staff. The CEO draws no salary; partners' field staff are paid by the partners and sit in the credit share.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: AMF's own breakdown, under 1%, in place of the shared default for goods programmes (@staff_pay.share_goods): its financials give its staff costs.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: AMF's staff are mostly UK-based charity staff: the shared gap for UK charity staff (@staff_pay.gap_uk_charity).

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid by cash donations
Units of value per dollar you give

output.label: Units of value per dollar you give
